body.text: Voters in Melbourne's Point Cook could help knock down Labor's red wall
In short:
Overcrowded schools and roads are shaping to be key election issues in the south-west Melbourne suburb of Point Cook.
Residents of the growth suburb have also been advocating for a public pool for a decade.
What's next?
Election day in Victoria is this Saturday, November 28.
Getting around in Point Cook, in Melbourne's south-west, is a challenge.
A survey of nearly 500 people conducted by Victoria's Big Build authority in April and May, as part of potential road upgrades, asked people about the last time they travelled on Point Cook Road.
A whopping 93 per cent of people said they had experienced congestion.
About 60 per cent of people said they felt unsafe or very unsafe, including people reporting road rage incidents when lanes merged.
Most said they saw extra lanes as the best solution.
At the morning drop off at Alamanda College, Mandy Mishra said local traffic is her top election issue.
"Point Cook Road gets very busy when I go to the office in the morning, so I have to leave at 630 in the morning," she said.
Another Alamanda parent, Nahid Rahman, said "Point Cook Road should have been doubled ten years ago".
"I've been living in Point Cook since 2007 — almost 20 years — one single road, and no improvements,"
Point Cook has become 'a problem' for Labor
When it comes to Melbourne's booming growth suburbs, Point Cook is one of the more established.
Homes have rapidly dotted the area since the 1990s.
The area south of the Princes Freeway, on the under-appreciated western side of the bay, is home to a RAAF base and an impressive array of birdlife.

In the past, the electorate of Point Cook, which also takes in the suburbs of Seabrook, Altona Meadows and Werribee South, would have been considered safe Labor territory, part of the party's so-called "red wall" across Melbourne's west and north.
But locals the growing pains felt by newer booming suburbs are still being felt in Point Cook.
Labor has promised $195 million to widen the road at Seabrook, and points to two upgraded intersections.
Work on Point Cook Road has not been featured among the Liberal Party's election promises.
Former political strategist and Redbridge Group pollster Kos Samaras told the ABC Point Cook was "in a group of seats which, in a normal election, should not be a problem" to win for Labor.
"But it's in a group of seats where it is now a problem, because of the battering that the Labor party is absorbing across the state."
The push for a pool
Despite claiming the title of Australia's biggest suburb, with a population of 66,781 at the 2021 census, Point Cook has no local pool.
The wait list for swimming lessons at the nearest pool, in Hoppers Crossing, can be up to a year.
The Point Cook Action Group, a residents' association, made a submission to the Wyndham City Council for a pool and indoor sports facility back in 2018.

"Point Cook is one of the largest suburbs across Australia, a lot of migrant population, and it's very important that people have swimming skills," said Senthill Sundaram, a spokesperson for the group.
"To be frank, we are really, really frustrated in Point Cook in terms of the lack of infrastructure."
Kalai Meeran moved to Point Cook from Sydney in 2025, and said her children, aged 16 and 13, were missing out on swimming lessons.
"We couldn't find anything in our suburb," she said.
"In Sydney, in every suburb there is a community pool … and it's run by councils."
Wyndham council runs pools at Hoppers Crossing and Werribee, which it concedes are exceeding capacity.
The council is advocating for $50 million in state and federal funds to build a new pool in West Tarneit, and $250,000 for planning for an indoor sports centre in Point Cook.
Council officers are also investigating demand for aquatic facilities, after acknowledging the push for a pool in Point Cook.
They are due to report back in March 2027.
The need for more schools
Back at Alamanda College, morning drop off is in full swing, with kids whizzing by on bikes and scooters, and parents hurrying their kids out of double-parked cars.
The kindergarten to year nine school is wildly popular with young families, with 87.5 per cent of parents giving it a positive endorsement, compared to the state average of 70.6 per cent.
But Alamanda has 3,237 students, according to its annual report, putting it among the biggest schools in the state.
"They need more schools," parent Kalyan Nagelli said.
"On busy days, there are close to thousands of cars coming in."
The school has staggered start times across its junior and senior students, and construction of a new three-storey classroom building is set to finish early next year.
Atul Jhamb and Shivani Arora moved from the other side of Melbourne to Point Cook.
"We heard a lot of good things about Alamanda school, and that was was our main motivation to move to Point Cook all the way from Clyde North," Mr Jhamb said.
But when their children were old enough to start year seven, the couple chose to send them both to Bacchus Marsh Grammar, at least an hour away on the bus.
Labor MP for Point Cook Mathew Hilakari said the area's P-9 schools would transition to P-6 and 7-12, if Labor is re-elected on Saturday.
The Coalition has said it will review that decision.
Locals also mention crime as a key concern, and the Point Cook Action Group also told the ABC residents wanted a full review of bus services across the west.
